title: Welding Processes — Theory and Safety Awareness
objective: Recognise at knowledge level the main welding-process families named in the occupational curriculum, their terminology, equipment categories, standards, hazards and common quality considerations without performing welding work.

curriculum_traceability.knowledge_topic: KM-06-KT04 — Gas, Arc, TIG, MIG Welding processes for flat welding

safety_boundary: Knowledge and safety-awareness only. This lesson does not provide welding setup, operating steps, parameter settings, ignition, electrode or consumable selection, gas settings, material-preparation procedures, or instructions for performing a weld. Practical welding belongs in authorised occupational training under competent supervision.

sections.heading: 1. Welding process families
sections.body: The occupational curriculum introduces gas, arc, TIG and MIG welding as process families. At knowledge level, learners should recognise that these processes use different equipment and methods to create welded joints.

sections.heading: 2. Terms, definitions and symbols
sections.body: Welding uses standard terminology and drawing symbols so that fabrication requirements can be communicated consistently. Learners should recognise that these symbols and terms must be interpreted against approved drawings, specifications and workplace requirements.

sections.heading: 3. Equipment, accessories and consumables
sections.body: Different welding processes involve different categories of equipment, accessories and consumables. Their suitability depends on the process, material, specification and authorised workplace procedure. This lesson develops recognition only, not equipment-selection or operating skill.

sections.heading: 4. Codes, standards and data sheets
sections.body: Welding work is controlled by engineering requirements, codes, standards and approved technical information. These documents help define what is acceptable for a particular job and must take priority over guesswork or informal practice.

sections.heading: 5. Hazards and risk awareness
sections.body: Welding environments can involve serious hazards including intense heat and light, fumes, electrical energy, hot material and fire risk. Practical work therefore requires appropriate training, workplace controls and competent supervision.

sections.heading: 6. Weld quality and defects
sections.body: A weld may have conditions that do not meet the required quality standard. Learners should understand that defects can affect acceptance, reliability and the need for inspection or testing, and that decisions must follow the applicable specification.

sections.heading: 7. Material preparation concept
sections.body: Approved welding work requires the material condition and joint requirements to be understood before practical work begins. The required preparation depends on the drawing, material, process and approved procedure; this lesson does not teach the practical preparation steps.

sections.heading: 8. Stop and refer
sections.body: If the welding process, material, specification, equipment condition or authorised procedure is uncertain, stop and refer the matter to a competent trainer or supervisor before practical work is attempted.
